newsitem.title: GERMANY: German institutes see deficit at 3.0 to 3.2 pct.
newsitem.headline: German institutes see deficit at 3.0 to 3.2 pct.

text.p: Germany's six leading economic research institutes forecast the nation's public sector deficit will be 3.0 to 3.2 percent of economic output this year, government sources said on Monday.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has vowed to slash the deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, to meet the convergence criteria for European monetary union (EMU).

In a semiannual report to be released on Tuesday, the six institutes say they have no doubt EMU will start on time on January 1, 1999, but they criticised the fixation on the 3.0 percent deficit target.

German GDP growth should be 2.25 percent in 1997, falling short of the government projection of 2.5 percent growth, but it should rebound to 2.75 percent next year, the sources said. Consumer price inflation, meanwhile, should remain subdued at 1.5 percent.
The institutes see German unemployment averaging 4.28 million in 1997, dropping to 4.16 million next year.
German institutes see deficit at 3.0 to 3.2 pct =2
Many indicators point to a timely start to EMU with a large group of participating countries, the sources quoted the report as saying.
Doubts that Germany could meet the convergence criteria this year have fueled speculation about a possible delay in the EMU start.

Persistent high unemployment is Bonn's major hindrance in reining in its deficit, boosting outlays for benefits as it depresses tax revenues. The government has forecast average unemployment would rise 200,000 this year from last year's 3.9 million.
